For your 2023 GasGas MC 250F, GasGas specifies:
- **Rider sag: 105 mm (4.13 in)** with you in full riding gear, feet on the pegs.
- **Static sag: 35 mm (1.38 in)** with the bike upright under its own weight, nobody aboard.

Both are measured from fully extended suspension, using the same rear-axle-to-fender points. Set rider sag first, then check static sag: too little static sag means the shock spring is too soft; too much means it’s too stiff.

Service sooner if damping becomes inconsistent, the fork starts leaking, or its action noticeably deteriorates—don’t wait for the interval with those symptoms.

That combination often means **too little support**, letting the fork ride deep where it feels harsh, then run out of travel on landings. Don’t automatically soften it.

1. **Fork air:** check cold with the front wheel off the ground. GASGAS’s stock reference is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**; establish that baseline if the pressure is unknown, and release trapped outer-chamber air through the bleeders—not the main air valve.
2. **Fork compression:** if it dives and uses deep travel even on ordinary bumps, turn compression **2 clicks in from your current position**. If currently at the stock **12 clicks out, try 10 out**. This is a general tuning test for more hold-up, not a factory preset.

Ride the same chop and a familiar landing for a few laps. Keep the change if it rides higher and becomes more comfortable; return to baseline if it deflects more without improving support. If chop improves but landings still overwhelm it, check spring pressure and end-stroke support before adding more compression.

What do you weigh in gear, and what air pressure are you running cold?

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork air pressure:** Check cold, front wheel unloaded; use 10.4 bar (151 psi) as the stock reference if the current baseline is unknown.
- **Fork compression:** If the fork dives and rides deep, turn 2 clicks in from the current setting; from 12 to 10 clicks out only if currently at stock.
Harsh on chop plus bottoming often means the fork lacks support and rides too deep—not that it needs softer compression. Establish cold air pressure before changing clickers.

Your fork needs more hold-up under braking—check the air spring before adding damping.

1. **Fork air:** GasGas’s stock reference is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**. Check cold with the front wheel off the ground; if below that, restore it and retest before changing clickers. Bleed the outer chambers separately—don’t release the main air spring.
2. **Fork compression:** If pressure is correct, turn compression **two clicks in from your current position**. Stock is 12 clicks out, so if you’re at stock, try **10 out**. Leave rebound alone; its stock reference is 12 out.

Also check chassis balance: GasGas specifies **105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag**. Too little rider sag puts extra load on the front.

While braking, stand and brace with your legs, hips back over the pegs, then squeeze the lever progressively. Practice five moderate straight-line stops at the same marker.

What do you weigh in riding gear? That determines whether the stock air-pressure reference needs moving. Retest the same braking zone; undo the compression change if it adds harshness without reducing dive.

- **Fork air pressure:** Check cold, front wheel unloaded; restore to 10.4 bar (151 psi) if below the stock reference.
- **Fork compression:** After confirming air pressure, turn two clicks in from current; if currently 12 clicks out, change from 12 to 10 clicks out.

Start with **1 click at a time** on your CRF250R—testers consistently find this generation sensitive to small adjustments. General tuning practice is 1–2 clicks, but start with one here.

- **Compression:** out is softer; in is firmer.
- **Rebound:** out returns faster; in returns slower.

Change only one adjuster, ride the same section for a few laps at a repeatable pace, then compare with your original setting. Write down each change; if it gets worse, return to baseline before trying anything else. Count positions out from lightly seated—never force the adjuster.

The shock’s high-speed compression uses turns, not clicks; don’t treat that outer adjuster like a clicker.
Change one click at a time on this CRF250R, testing one adjuster over the same section.

**That isn’t normal—the shock is losing damping as it heats up.** The spring doesn’t suddenly get softer; reduced compression damping lets it sink farther, and reduced rebound damping makes it bounce.

Most likely causes, in order:
1. Degraded or aerated shock oil losing damping when hot.
2. Low nitrogen charge or a leaking gas seal allowing the oil to foam.
3. Internal seal or piston wear letting hot, thinner oil bypass the damping circuits.

**First, with the bike cold and secured, inspect the shock shaft, seal area and reservoir for oil wetness or damage.** A dry shock doesn’t rule out an internal fault. If you’ve already noticed the rear riding lower after the problem starts, Honda specifically calls for checking nitrogen loss.

Don’t stiffen the clickers to hide it or run another long moto to reproduce it. Have a suspension shop check the charge, oil and internal seals; charging and opening the pressurized shock require proper equipment.
Soft and bouncy after 20 minutes points to heat-related damping fade, not a spring or clicker problem. Inspect for leakage, then have the shock serviced and its nitrogen charge checked.

Yes—the tire is the first cushion between the ground and your suspension. Pressure can make a good fork or shock feel harsh or vague without changing the damping itself.

- **Higher pressure:** firmer feel, more chatter and deflection, but better protection against rim strikes and pinch flats.
- **Lower pressure:** more compliance and grip, but too low feels vague or squirmy and risks rim damage.

Honda’s cold baseline for your 2023 CRF450R is **100 kPa (15 psi) front and rear**. Set that before judging suspension settings. As general tuning practice, test about **1 psi at a time**: lower for smooth, slick ground or deep sand; higher for rocks, square edges and hard landings. Leave the clickers alone during that test so you can feel the difference.

Stop lowering pressure if you feel a rim strike or tire squirm. Check pressures cold at the riding location; don’t bleed a hot tire back down to the cold figure.

**Your shock spring is likely too soft.** Getting 105 mm rider sag has taken enough preload that the rear barely settles under the bike’s own weight.

GasGas specifies **105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag**. Your 20 mm static sag is 15 mm short of that target. Assuming the linkage moves freely and the measurements repeat, the fix is a **stiffer shock spring—not more preload or different clickers**. Simply backing off preload will increase rider sag beyond the target.

Before buying a spring, repeat the measurement after pushing the rear down, then after lifting it and letting it settle. A large difference points to binding or bearing friction that needs checking first.

What shock spring rate is fitted, and what do you weigh in full riding gear? Those determine how far stiffer to go; after fitting, reset rider sag to 105 mm and check that static sag comes close to 35 mm.
With 105 mm rider sag but only 20 mm static sag, the shock spring is likely too soft and needs excessive preload to support you.

On your 2023 CRF450R’s **standard shock spring, 56 N/mm, do not shorten the installed spring below 222.9 mm (8.78 in)**. Measure the spring itself between its seats with the rear wheel off the ground—not the exposed threads above the collar.

Honda’s figures are:
- Installed spring length: **222.9–233 mm (8.78–9.20 in)**; standard setting **232.3 mm (9.15 in)**.
- One collar turn: **1.5 mm of spring-length change**, adding or removing **84 N of preload**.
- Rider sag target: **105 mm**, seated in normal riding position, wearing full gear.

Shortening the spring adds preload and reduces sag; it does **not** increase the spring rate. If you cannot reach 105 mm sag without going below the minimum length, you need a stiffer shock spring—not more collar turns.

Honda does not publish a static-sag target for this bike. As general guidance, roughly **30–40 mm** is a useful check: very little static sag with correct rider sag points to a spring that is too soft.
On the stock shock spring, too much preload means shortening its installed length below 222.9 mm—or needing excessive preload to achieve the correct sag.

Most often it’s **measurement or load changing—not the spring changing rate**. Your CRF250R’s standard rider sag is **105 mm (4.1 in)** with the standard shock spring.

Likely causes, in order:
- **Different measuring conditions:** riding gear, fuel, packed-on mud, body position, or a different helper can move the reading.
- **Preload collar moving:** if the locking collar isn’t secure, spring preload can change between rides. Put a witness mark across the collars to spot movement.
- **Linkage or shock friction:** the rear stops at different heights depending on whether you pushed it down or lifted it first. Dry or binding bearings can cause this.
- **Fresh suspension settling:** some initial drift is possible; continued changes need checking.

**First check:** on level ground with the same gear, fuel load and rider position, repeat the measurement between the left rear-fender bolt center and chain-adjuster locknut center. Subtract rider-loaded length from rear-wheel-off-ground length. Compare readings after gently pushing the rear down and after lifting it, letting it settle each time. Don’t chase inconsistent readings with preload.

How many millimeters is it changing between rides? If there’s bearing play, a knock, leakage or a loose collar, fix that before riding.
Changing sag usually comes from inconsistent measuring, changing load, a moving preload collar, or suspension friction. Repeat the measurement consistently before changing preload again.

**Bleed them after practice and between motos.** Your Showa forks use coil springs—you’re releasing trapped pressure, not setting an air-spring pressure.

1. With the engine off, put the bike securely on a stand so the **front wheel is off the ground and the forks are fully extended**. Let the forks cool first.
2. Clean around the small air-release screw on top of each fork leg. Don’t loosen the large fork caps or the damping adjusters.
3. Slowly loosen each air-release screw until any hiss stops. You don’t need to remove the screws.
4. Gently snug both screws again—don’t crank them down. If one leaks afterward, check its sealing O-ring.

Don’t bleed them with the bike’s weight compressing the forks; that can leave a vacuum when they extend.

For a guided walkthrough, tap **“Working on the bike?”** above the message box and choose **“Release built-up air from the fork.”**
Release built-up fork air after practice and between motos, with the front wheel off the ground and the forks fully extended.

**A full air-side service means servicing the left-leg air cartridge—not just opening the fork bleeders.** On your 2023 MC 250F’s WP XACT AER, separate these jobs:

- **Routine care:** with the fork cold and front wheel off the ground, release trapped outer-chamber air through both bleeder screws, then close them. Clean the dust boots and tubes, keeping oil off the brake disc. This does **not** depressurize the main air spring.
- **Left outer-leg oil:** GASGAS specifies **230 +10 ml (7.78 +0.34 fl oz) of SAE 4 fork oil**. That is outer-leg lubrication oil—not an air-cartridge fill quantity.
- **Air-cartridge service:** inspect the air-piston seals, sliding surfaces and pressure-equalization system, replacing worn seals and renewing the specified lubricant. The exact cartridge teardown, tooling and reassembly procedure isn't confirmed here, so those oil figures alone aren't enough to walk you through it safely.

A too-tight chain doesn’t just wear faster—it can **fight the rear suspension and overload the drivetrain**.

The rear axle moves in an arc around the swingarm pivot. As the suspension compresses, the distance between the front sprocket and rear axle increases until the countershaft, swingarm pivot and axle line up. The chain needs enough slack to accommodate that movement.

Without it:
- **Suspension binds:** the rear can feel harsh and lose grip over bumps.
- **Bearing loads climb:** the countershaft and rear-wheel bearings take excessive pull, even without much throttle.
- **Parts wear or fail:** the chain, sprockets and swingarm slider suffer; in severe cases the chain can break.

| Terrain tire | Choose it when… | Why it works |
|---|---|---|

| **Hard** | Your finger won’t push in; the surface is compacted, shiny or blue-grooved | Lower, closely spaced knobs put more rubber on the ground and resist folding |

1. Secure the bike on a stand with the wheel clear. Spin it and watch the rim for side-to-side wobble or an up-and-down hop.

3. Lightly tap each spoke with a spoke wrench. Compare spokes on the **same side** of the wheel: a noticeably dull note can flag a loose one, but sound alone doesn’t set tension.
4. Use a correctly fitting spoke wrench and a spoke torque wrench where possible. Bring loose spokes up gradually in small passes around the wheel, rechecking rim straightness. Don’t force a seized nipple or tighten every spoke just to make them sound identical.

If several spokes are very loose, the rim visibly wobbles, or anything is cracked or broken, have the wheel trued before riding. Honda calls for wheel inspection **each race or about 2.5 hours**; recheck after the first ride following adjustment.

Start with **Honda’s stock baseline**, not an aggressive race setup. Record what’s on the bike first; these suspension settings assume stock components.

1. **Fork:** set compression to **12 clicks out** and rebound to **13 clicks out**, both legs equal. Release built-up air with the front wheel off the ground and fork fully extended.
2. **Shock:** set low-speed compression to **6 clicks out**, high-speed compression to **2 1/6 turns out**, and rebound to **11 clicks out**. Set rider sag to **105 mm (4.1 in)** wearing your riding gear. Count adjusters out from lightly seated—never force them.
3. **Tires:** set both cold to **100 kPa (15 psi)**.
4. **Chain:** check **65–70 mm (2 1/2–2 3/4 in)** with the rear wheel off the ground, lifting the chain and measuring from the swingarm top to the chain-pin center at the rear end of the slider.
5. **Controls:** throttle free play **2–6 mm** at the grip flange; clutch free play **10–20 mm** at the lever tip. Position bars and levers so your wrists stay comfortable standing.

Check oil, cold coolant, filter seating, spokes, axle security and brake feel. **Don’t ride with a sticking throttle, suspect brakes or fluid leaks.**

**Suspension is the biggest comfort upgrade on your 2023 450 SX-F—not a softer seat.** Testers consistently find this generation’s chassis stiff, and several report harshness from the air fork over small braking bumps.

My spending order for a vet rider:

1. **Correct springs, sag and a vet-paced suspension tune.** KTM’s starting targets are **105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag**. The stock US fork-air reference is **10.7 bar (155 psi)**; adjust for weight and travel use rather than simply dropping pressure—riding too deep can make it harsher.
2. **A coil-cartridge conversion if the air fork still beats you up.** A commonly used choice is the **WP XACT PRO 6500**, sprung and valved for your pace; confirm the kit fits your exact year. Repeated tuner and rider experience favors coil conversions for small-bump comfort and consistency, with added weight and cost as the trade-off.
3. **Controls that let you relax.** Set bar position and lever angle so you can stand with loose hands and neutral wrists. Softer grips help vibration, but won’t fix harsh suspension.

**My pick: pay for a weight-matched suspension setup first; choose the coil conversion before chasing clamps, mounts or engine power.**
